extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career TV writers, showrunners, and people interested in TV sitcom writing practice
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria about how sitcom scripts should be produced and how young TV writers should be trained — weighing writers' room practices vs solo drafting and mentorship responsibilities. Focused on professional TV sitcom writing and staff development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young writers must write drafts themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Young writers need to write drafts by themselves for their own development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine argues that if you’re a young writer on staff YOU need to come up with big jokes that end scenes, make adjustments when the story outline doesn’t work, write tender speeches, and then do the rewrite — finding better jokes and more artful story turns. The point is hands-on experience producing first drafts and carrying a script through rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop specific craft skills through ownership of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking responsibility for a script (writing first drafts and doing rewrites) develops essential skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skills listed include inventing 'big jokes,' solving thorny story issues, satisfying notes you may disagree with, and discovering more artful story turns. The post emphasizes pressure, responsibility, and more work as necessary for growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of authorship/ownership (retain original material)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is real pride and learning value in having a large portion of your original script make it to air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine: 'There’s a real sense of author’s pride when 90% of your script makes it to air. And it’s a real learning experience when only 10% does.' The criterion values both outcomes as part of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: room-written scripts can erode individual ability
rubrics_metrics.description: While group-written shows can be consistently funny, they can erode a young writer’s confidence and solo-writing ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chuck Lorre shows and other table-written systems produce funny episodes but young staff may report, after two years, that they 'couldn’t write a script on his own again.' Levine warns the system can make writers feel worse about their own skills rather than better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor in rooms reduces breadth of skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers’ rooms tend to let specialists (the 'big joke guy' or the 'story guy') handle specific tasks, which can limit each writer’s holistic development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine notes you can 'zone out' during parts of the room process and rejoin when an issue is resolved; this compartmentalization means writers may not learn to generate both story fixes and killer jokes themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showrunners’ responsibility to mentor and require drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Showrunners should (optionally, but ideally) see mentoring as part of their role and insist young writers produce drafts to learn the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine frames mentorship as paying it forward: he learned from Jim Brooks and others and believes showrunners should give outline notes, second-draft notes, and rewrite drafts. It's acknowledged as more work for the showrunner but 'worth it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term benefit of grooming writers (succession/assumption of roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grooming young writers yields practical benefits: over time they can assume more important roles and allow a showrunner to step away a little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine points to succession and career development as self-serving but valid reasons to mentor: trained staff can carry the show forward and fill larger roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creators often retain responsibility for emotional arcs; writers tasked with comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: On many shows, creators handle emotional moments, arcs, and series direction, while staff writers are told 'Comedy is King' and primarily supply jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine cites FRIENDS and other shows where creators did the heavy lifting on emotional/arc material and staff were instructed to 'pepper the show with killer jokes.' This is a criterion about role allocation and what counts as a writer’s remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-draft generation method impacts credit and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether first drafts are written solo (sent out to a writer) or born 'at the table' by committee affects both who gets credit and how writers learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine contrasts FRIENDS (writers sent out to craft first drafts, then staff rewrites) with Chuck Lorre shows (first drafts written at the table by committee, writers’ names assigned afterward), noting the learning implications and how 'no writer ever gets to do a first draft' under some systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pair or small-team writing as a middle ground
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-person team dynamic can balance the benefits of solo work and a large writers' room, promoting mutual learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters describe pairs where one partner generates ideas and the other shapes structure/dialogue; with only two people both remain active participants and both learn more than in a larger group where it's easy to tune out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and authenticity of credits vs 'room-written' resumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Room-written credit practices can lead to misleading resumes; industry employers may value 'works well in a room' differently than solo authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raise the anti-pattern that some writers 'get their name put on a script' despite limited contribution, creating 'b.s. resumes.' This is an evaluative concern about fairness, hiring, and how credits reflect ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showrunner priority trade-off: best show vs teaching writers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a legitimate tension between a showrunner’s duty to produce the best show and the desire/obligation to train young writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levine acknowledges that a showrunner might argue 'his job wasn’t to teach young writers but to turn out the best shows he can,' but counters with the importance of mentorship and 'paying it forward.' This frames an organizational criterion for how a writers' room is structured.
